analysis.one_liner: Lets the Labor Department penalize employer health plans that shortchange mental health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let the Labor Department fine employer health plans that fail to cover mental health and substance use care equally, never received a House vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires employer health plans to cover mental health and substance use treatment on the same terms as physical health care, but the Labor Department currently has no power to impose penalties when plans break that rule — it can only sue in court. This bill would change the law so the Department could directly fine employers and insurers whose plans violate the mental health parity requirement. The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee in February 2021 and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families with employer-sponsored health insurance who need mental health or substance use treatment. If the bill passed, plans that charge higher copays, tighter limits, or stricter prior-approval rules for mental health care than for medical care could be fined directly by the Labor Department, giving patients a faster remedy than a private lawsuit and giving employers and insurers a real financial reason to comply with parity rules.

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, the Labor Department can enforce mental health parity in employer group health plans only through lawsuits; this bill amends ERISA so the Department can impose civil penalties directly on plan sponsors and insurers for any failure to meet the parity requirements of section 712.
The penalty authority would apply to group health plans for plan years beginning one year after enactment, giving employers and insurers time to come into compliance before fines could start.

The same change extends the Department's direct-penalty authority to violations of the existing rules restricting plans' use of genetic information, folding two compliance areas into one enforcement pathway.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor self-insured health plans and the insurers that administer employer coverage would bear the cost. Those found violating parity rules could face civil penalties, and all covered plans would face the compliance cost of auditing whether their mental health benefits are truly on par with medical benefits. Some of that cost could be passed into premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies only to employer group health plans under ERISA; it does nothing for people who buy coverage on their own or rely on public programs, and it does not itself add mental health providers — it only penalizes plans that treat mental health care unequally.

Civil penalties and parity audits impose real compliance costs on employers and insurers, and those costs can ultimately flow into premiums paid by workers, which is the trade-off any enforcement bill of this kind makes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a narrow, targeted fix to a known enforcement gap: the parity requirement already exists, and the bill only adds a standard government enforcement tool — civil penalties — that the Labor Department already has for other plan violations like genetic information rules. The main cost falls on noncompliant plans and on employers' compliance efforts, with some risk of premium pass-through. The bill does not expand who is covered or add providers, so its benefit is limited to people in ERISA-covered employer plans. On balance, a modest, well-designed bill whose cost is proportionate to its purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and never came up again, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross introduced the Parity Enforcement Act of 2021 on February 25, 2021, joined by Reps. Courtney, Fitzpatrick, and Kuster as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
The bill attracted 15 cosponsors, 14 Democrats and 1 Republican, but the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever occurred after the referral.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired in committee without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employer plan sponsors and health insurers are better off because the bill died: they continue to face mental health parity obligations only through lawsuits rather than direct Labor Department fines, and enforcement of parity for the roughly half of Americans with employer coverage remains weaker than supporters said it should be.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start — 14 of its 15 cosponsors were Democrats and 1, Rep. Fitzpatrick, was a Republican — and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no partisan split on the merits; its death in committee leaves the actual opponents unidentified.

industries.industry: Employer health plan sponsors and health insurers
industries.note: The bill would have let the Labor Department fine them directly for failing to cover mental health and substance use care on par with medical care, adding both penalty exposure and audit costs. Today those plans face parity obligations mainly through lawsuits, so noncompliance carries little direct financial risk — the bill's death keeps it that way.

industries.industry: Mental health and substance use treatment providers
industries.note: Stronger parity enforcement could mean fewer coverage denials and higher-cost-sharing barriers, increasing the likelihood that patients can actually use their benefits and pay for treatment. The bill contains no provider payment provisions of its own.
